runs.goal: find out how tall the Starship launch tower at Starbase is
runs.detail: The Starbase launch towers are about 145 meters tall, roughly 475 to 480 feet. The original tower is usually given as about 146 meters. The newer Pad B tower is officially 144.5 meters. Both stand about 20 meters taller than the full Starship stack.

sections.heading: Tower 1 (Pad A, the original tower)
points: The original Orbital Launch and Integration Tower at Starbase is most often given as about 146 m (480 ft) tall.
Some trackers using official permit filings give a slightly lower figure of about 143 m (about 469 ft), so treat it as roughly 143–146 m.
It has the 'chopstick' arms used to stack the rocket and catch Super Heavy boosters. Pad A was used for Flights 1 through 11.

sections.heading: Tower 2 (Pad B / Pad 2)
points: The newer tower at Pad B is officially listed at 474 ft (144.5 m).
Its base is about 1.5 m taller than Tower 1's, which fits the slightly taller Block 3 boosters.
Pad B is the pad used for Block 3 test flights.

sections.heading: For scale
points: A full Starship stack is about 124 m (408 ft) tall, so the tower stands about 20 m above the rocket.

runs.goal: find out how the most recent Starship booster catch compares to the first booster catch
runs.detail: The first booster catch was smooth, on Flight 5 in October 2024. The latest successful one, Flight 8 in March 2025, worked even though some engines didn't relight, and that booster was later flown again. Last week, Flight 15's new V3 booster called off its catch and was lost.

sections.heading: Which catches we're comparing
points: First booster catch: Flight 5, October 13, 2024, Super Heavy Booster 12 (Block 1). The Mechazilla tower's chopstick arms caught it on SpaceX's first attempt.
Most recent successful catch: Flight 8, March 6, 2025, Booster 15. It was the third catch, after Booster 14 on Flight 7 (January 16, 2025).
The tower has caught 3 boosters in 4 attempts. Flight 6 (November 2024) called off its catch after losing communication with the tower, and the booster landed in the Gulf instead.
Most recent attempt: Flight 15, November 13, 2026, Booster 22. This was the first V3 booster sent back for a catch. It aborted on its own and was lost in the Gulf.

sections.heading: Flight 5 (first catch)
points: Booster 12 flew with Ship 30. It returned to the launch site and was caught about 7 minutes after liftoff.
The ship also completed its flight and made a controlled splashdown in the Indian Ocean, so both stages of the flight succeeded.
Booster 12 was never reflown. It was retired to the Rocket Garden at Starbase.

sections.heading: Flight 8 (latest successful catch)
points: Engines were the main difference. Only 11 of 13 planned engines relit for the boostback burn, and 12 of 13 relit for the landing burn. SpaceX still cleared the catch, and the three center engines guided the booster into the arms.
Booster 15 approached the tower with less sideways motion than earlier catches, which made for a more direct approach.
The rest of the flight went worse than Flight 5. Ship 34 was lost after four of its six engines shut down early. SpaceX later traced the booster's relight problems to the engine igniters overheating.
Booster 15 was later reflown and expended on Flight 11 in 2025, so this catch led to booster reuse, which Flight 5 never did.

sections.heading: Flight 15 (latest attempt, no catch)
points: The tower and flight controllers were go for a catch. Then Booster 22's guidance software found the booster was low on fuel and off course, so it aborted and diverted to a splashdown in the Gulf, where it was lost.
Ship 42 was caught by the tower about 22.5 hours after launch. That was the first catch of an upper stage returning from orbit.
A V3 Super Heavy booster has not been caught yet.

sections.heading: Bottom line
points: Flight 5 went cleanly on the first try. Flight 8 showed a catch can still work when several engines fail to relight. The newest V3 booster has not repeated either result.

Booster 12's catch went smoothly, and its ship also finished the flight. Booster 15 was caught even though several engines failed to relight, but its ship was lost. Booster 15 was later reflown. The latest attempt, Booster 22 on Flight 15 (November 2026), aborted because it was low on fuel and off course. It was lost in the Gulf, though the tower caught the ship.

runs.goal: find out how the most recent Starship booster catch compares to the first booster catch
runs.detail: The most recent booster catch was Booster 15 on Flight 8, in March 2025. Two of its boostback engines failed, but it came in steadier than the first catch in 2024, and it later flew again. The newer V3 booster's first catch try, on Flight 15, was called off because of a low-fuel alarm.

sections.heading: Catch history at a glance
points: Flight 5, 13 Oct 2024, Booster 12: first ever chopstick catch, a success.
Flight 7, 16 Jan 2025, Booster 14: second successful catch. Booster 14 later flew again.
Flight 8, 6 Mar 2025, Booster 15: third successful catch, and the most recent one. SpaceX had then landed three of four catch attempts.
Flights 12 to 14 (May to Sept 2026) used the new Version 3 boosters, which ended in the Gulf with no catch.

Flight 15, 13 Nov 2026, Booster 22: the first try at catching a V3 booster with Raptor 3 engines. The flight computer called it off because of a low-fuel alarm, and the booster blew up offshore. The Ship upper stage was caught by the tower for the first time on 14 Nov.

sections.heading: First catch (Flight 5, Booster 12)
points: Flew back after boostback, slid sideways between the chopsticks and was caught about seven minutes after liftoff.
The chopsticks then put B12 back on the launch mount so the leftover fuel could be drained.
The upper stage, Ship 30, finished its flight and came down in the Indian Ocean.
B12 had damage to one of its chine sections. It was never flown again and now sits in the Rocket Garden.

sections.heading: Latest successful catch (Flight 8, Booster 15)
points: Only 11 of the 13 boostback engines lit, but the booster still made it back to the tower.
It came in with less sideways motion than earlier catches and was caught cleanly.
The upper stage, Ship 34, was lost soon after. Four of its six engines shut down too early.
Booster 15 was flown again and expended on Flight 11. It was the second Super Heavy to fly twice.

sections.heading: Key differences
points: Both are Block 1/2 boosters about 71 m tall with Raptor 2 engines. The catch method was the same.
Flight 8 had the harder ride home, with engines out on boostback, yet its approach was more controlled and less sideways.
Reuse: B12 was retired, while B15 flew a second time. This shows the program moving toward reusable boosters.
Upper stage: Flight 5's ship worked well, but Flight 8's ship was destroyed.
The newer V3 booster is 72.3 m tall and has not been caught yet. The Flight 15 abort means V3 still needs its first catch.

input.summary: SpaceX's most recent successful Super Heavy catch was Booster 15 on Flight 8 (March 6, 2025), its third catch. The first was Booster 12 on Flight 5 (October 13, 2024). Flight 8 lost two boostback engines but came in with less sideways motion. B15 was later flown again, while B12 was retired with chine damage. The latest attempt was on Flight 15 (November 13, 2026), the first try with a V3 booster. It was called off because of a low-fuel alarm, so the booster was lost.

runs.goal: find out what the James Webb Space Telescope's mirror is made of and why
runs.detail: Webb's mirror is 18 hexagon-shaped beryllium segments with a very thin gold coating. Beryllium is light and stiff, and it keeps its shape in deep cold. Gold reflects about 99 percent of infrared light, which is what Webb sees. I couldn't save the notes because Notion is off.

sections.heading: What the mirror is made of
points: The 6.5 m primary mirror is built from 18 hexagonal segments that fit together into a roughly circular shape.
Each segment is made of beryllium, a light metal (symbol Be), held by a beryllium support frame. Each piece weighs about 20 kg (46 lb) on Earth.
The segments are coated with a very thin layer of gold, which is then covered by a thin protective glass-like overcoat.
The beryllium was mined in Utah and purified in Ohio. The gold was applied by vacuum vapor deposition: the gold is vaporized in a vacuum chamber and settles onto the polished surface.

sections.heading: Why beryllium
points: It is strong and stiff but very light, which matters for a large mirror that has to be launched and then unfold in space.
It holds its shape at cryogenic temperatures. Webb works below about −400°F, and many materials warp at that temperature.
It can survive the shaking of launch and stay precisely aligned, so all 18 segments work like a single large mirror.

sections.heading: Why gold
points: Webb is an infrared telescope, and gold reflects infrared light extremely well, about 99% compared with roughly 85–95% for silver or aluminum.
Gold reflects highly across a very wide range of wavelengths, so the mirror catches as many faint photons as possible from very distant objects.
Gold does not react easily, so it does not tarnish. The overcoat on top also protects it.

input.summary: Webb's 6.5-meter primary mirror is made of 18 hexagonal segments of beryllium, each coated with a very thin layer of gold and a protective overcoat. Beryllium was chosen because it is strong, stiff, and light, and it keeps its shape in the extreme cold where Webb works. Gold was added because it reflects about 99% of infrared light, the light Webb is built to see, and it does not tarnish.
input.title: What the James Webb Space Telescope's mirror is made of and why

runs.goal: find out what the James Webb Space Telescope's mirror is made of and why
runs.detail: Webb's mirror is made of 18 beryllium segments, each with a very thin coat of gold. Beryllium is light and stiff and keeps its shape in deep cold. Gold reflects infrared light very well, and infrared is what Webb looks at.

sections.heading: What the mirror is made of
points: The primary mirror is about 6.5 m (21 ft) across and is made of 18 hexagonal segments.
Each segment is made of beryllium, a light, stiff metal, and sits in a beryllium support frame. Each segment weighs about 20 kg (46 lb).
The reflecting surface is polished very smooth and then given a very thin coat of pure gold, about 100 nanometres thick. Only about 50 grams of gold is used for the whole mirror.
A thin, clear glass layer (amorphous silica) covers the soft gold to protect it.
The beryllium was mined in Utah and purified in Ohio.

sections.heading: Why beryllium
points: It is strong and stiff but very light, which matters for a large mirror that has to be launched on a rocket.
It holds its shape at cryogenic temperatures, below about -400°F, where Webb works. Its behaviour in the cold is stable and predictable, so the mirror stays in focus.
The segments also have to survive the shaking of launch and then stay lined up as one large mirror.

sections.heading: Why gold
points: Webb observes mainly in infrared light, unlike Hubble, which works mostly in visible light.
Gold reflects infrared light very well across a wide range of wavelengths, so the gold coat helps the mirror collect as much of that light as possible.
The gold is only a coating. The mirror is not solid gold.

sections.heading: Why hexagons
points: Hexagons fit together without gaps, so the 18 segments together make a mirror that is roughly circular.
Using segments let the large mirror fold up to fit inside the rocket and then open out in space.

Gold was chosen because it reflects infrared light very well, and infrared is the light Webb is built to see.
